clue.text: Judge served in the military after retirement? That's a puzzle

indicators.note: retirement means going backwards, so the words served in the military are read in reverse

parts.note: served in the sense of was, as in 'served as captain'
a GI is an American soldier, someone in the military

explanation.surface: An old soldier turned judge, after leaving the forces, is a bit of a mystery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after retirement' suggests a pensioner but signals going backwards; GI is the usual American soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: A jigsaw is a picture-assembly game, one kind of puzzle.

clue.text: Bishop, needing place of work, fills in card -—- he claims an allowance

indicators.note: the bishop and his place go into the card, filling it

parts.note: the joker is a playing card
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
a see is a bishop's diocese, his place of work

explanation.surface: A bishop filling in a form to claim a benefit.
explanation.walkthrough: A see, a diocese, is fittingly a bishop's own place of work.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain someone out of work claims jobseeker's allowance, a state benefit paid while looking for employment.

clue.text: Stomach sixty minutes with one European folk-singer

parts.note: gut means stomach
sixty minutes is an hour, abbreviated HR
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A folk-singer stomaching an hour in the company of a European.
explanation.definitionFit: Woody Guthrie (and his son Arlo) are famous American folk musicians.

clue.text: Navy with explosive in American battle

indicators.note: the navy and the explosive go in the American abbreviation

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy
HE is high explosive

explanation.surface: Sailors with explosives fighting an American battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnhem was a 1944 Second World War battle in the Netherlands.

clue.text: Ireland's safeguarding politician's powers

indicators.note: Ireland's letters wrap protectively round the politician

parts.note: Eire is Ireland, here with its possessive S
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: Ireland protecting a politician's authority.
explanation.definitionFit: Empires are great states or realms, so powers in the sense of nations.

clue.text: Lines, say, written in cathedral city

indicators.note: the example abbreviation is put in the city's name

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire
say means for example, EG

explanation.surface: Lines of verse written in some cathedral town.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegy is a mournful poem, a set of lines of verse.

clue.text: Organised probe into wage for working youngster

indicators.note: the rearranged probe goes into the pay

parts.note: a wage is pay

indicators.note: organised means arranged anew, so the word probe is rearranged

explanation.surface: An organised investigation into wages paid to young workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organised' reshuffles the five letters of the word probe.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy delivering newspapers is a typical young person with a job.

clue.text: Once more let in to study at American college

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it
MIT is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology

explanation.surface: A student allowed back to study at an American university.
explanation.definitionFit: Readmit means admit again, to allow entry a second time.

clue.text: Secretly watch lad absorbing Playboy cover to cover?

indicators.note: the son takes in the outer letters

parts.note: a lad is a son

indicators.note: the two covers of the magazine name are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A boy reading a racy magazine from end to end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cover to cover' gives P and Y from Playboy; 'absorbing' puts them in SON.
explanation.definitionFit: To spy on someone is to observe them covertly.

clue.text: Container ready to be held up at start of experiment?

definitions.text: Container ready to be held up at start of experiment?
definitions.note: a glass vessel a chemist holds up to the light as a trial begins

indicators.note: in a down clue, held up means the words are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a butt is a large cask, a container
set means ready, as in 'ready, steady, go'

indicators.note: the start of the word experiment is its first letter

explanation.surface: A laboratory vessel poised for use as an experiment begins.
explanation.walkthrough: Read upwards, BUTT then SET become TESTTUB; the whole clue also describes the vessel itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A test tube is the narrow glass laboratory vessel a chemist raises when an experiment begins.

clue.text: Don't declare weapon

definitions.meaning: in cricket, a side that does not declare will ...
a truncheon or club carried by police

explanation.surface: Keep a weapon secret from customs.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a captain can declare, ending the innings early; not doing so means the side carries on batting.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it is cricket's alternative to declaring; as one word, a police truncheon.

clue.text: Devon flower girl out of place as model

parts.note: a flower is something that flows, a river; the Exe flows through Devon

indicators.note: the girl sits outside the place abbreviation

parts.note: Mary is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl from Devon selling flowers is a model citizen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' is a river, a crossword favourite; 'out of' means the girl goes outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Exemplary describes something serving as a pattern to copy, as a model does.

clue.text: One who composed in unconventional style, seriously

indicators.note: the composer goes in the rearranged letters
unconventional means not in the usual order, so the letters of style are rearranged

parts.note: Thomas Arne was the English composer of Rule, Britannia!

explanation.surface: A composer writing in an unorthodox manner, but meaning it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unconventional' reorders the letters of style into ESTLY, and the composer slots in after the first of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnestly means with sincere intent, gravely, not in jest.

clue.text: Italian person getting in from Ancona

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words from Ancona

explanation.surface: An Italian arriving from the Adriatic port of Ancona.
explanation.definitionFit: A citizen of Rome is an Italian, a specific example of one.

clue.text: Poetic ship taking sounding in this canal

indicators.note: sounding signals that the ship word is said aloud

parts.note: in poetry a keel stands for a whole ship

explanation.surface: A ship measuring depth as it passes through a canal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sounding' also suggests measuring water depth, apt for a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kiel Canal is a German waterway linking the North Sea and the Baltic.

clue.text: Begin to lack control, in a way, when drunk

parts.note: to run a business is to control it

indicators.note: a drunk slurs speech, so the phrase for in a way is said with a slur

parts.note: sort of means in a way, to some degree

explanation.surface: Someone losing their grip after too many drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when drunk' is a playful homophone signal: a tipsy speaker's S slurs to SH, turning SORT OF into SHORT OF.
explanation.definitionFit: To run short of something is to start not having enough of it.

clue.text: Tory gets in thanks finally to newspaper chiefs having given support

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of thanks
the Tory abbreviation is put in among the other letters

parts.note: two editors, each abbreviated ED
CON is short for Conservative, a Tory

explanation.surface: A Conservative gets into print thanks to supportive newspaper bosses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'newspaper chiefs' is plural, so editors twice; the Tory goes in after the first E.
explanation.definitionFit: To second a motion is to back it formally, so seconded means having backed it.

clue.text: Leaves one cold apartment near Victoria?

definitions.note: fails to impress or amuse anyone

indicators.note: near means the apartment sits right beside the falls

parts.note: Victoria Falls is the great waterfall on the Zambezi, so Victoria stands for falls
an apartment is a flat

explanation.surface: A chilly flat near London's Victoria station.
explanation.walkthrough: Victoria suggests the London district, but it means Victoria Falls on the Zambezi; the question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that falls flat fails to impress, leaving an audience unmoved.

clue.text: Runner more self-satisfied crossing line

indicators.note: the comparative word goes across the line letter, holding it

parts.note: smugger means more complacent

explanation.surface: A cocky athlete crossing the finishing line.
explanation.walkthrough: A runner here is one who runs contraband.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who runs goods illegally across borders is a smuggler, as in gun-runner.

clue.text: Advise daughter to leave course after vacation and make a fresh start

indicators.note: the daughter abbreviation departs from the advising word

parts.note: to recommend is to advise

indicators.note: vacating course empties out its middle, leaving the outer letters

explanation.surface: Telling a daughter to quit her course and begin again after the holidays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after vacation' looks like holiday time but means emptying: course loses OURS, leaving CE.
explanation.definitionFit: To recommence is to begin again, starting anew.

clue.text: Unscrupulous sort not unknown in court

indicators.note: not means the unknown is taken out of the court

parts.note: Chancery is a division of the English High Court
Y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A shady character well known in the law courts.
explanation.definitionFit: A chancer is an opportunist who takes risks with little regard for scruple.

clue.text: Gemstone or pearl, oddly

indicators.note: oddly picks the odd-numbered letters of or pearl

explanation.surface: Choosing between two jewels.
explanation.definitionFit: An opal is an iridescent precious stone.

clue.text: Get expert treatment that's successful

parts.note: a pro is a professional, an expert
a cure is medical treatment that works

explanation.surface: Seeking specialist medical care that actually works.
explanation.definitionFit: To procure is to obtain, acquire something.

clue.text: They say French cheeses give you wind

indicators.note: they say signals a word that is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: Brie is a soft French cheese; bries is the plural

explanation.surface: A joke about soft cheese causing flatulence.
explanation.definitionFit: A breeze is a light wind.

clue.text: Parking Sierra almost results in crash

parts.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

indicators.note: almost drops the last letter

parts.note: a sierra is a mountain range

explanation.surface: Parking a Ford Sierra car ends in a collision.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sierra was a popular Ford car; here it is a mountain range. PRANG is British slang for a minor collision.
explanation.definitionFit: Prang is British slang for a crash, especially a minor car accident.

clue.text: Course in Italian history followed by top academic stream

parts.note: history is the past
British schools often split pupils into streams, the A stream being the top

explanation.surface: A course of study in Italian history for the brightest students.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' suggests study, but it is a course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasta is a dish served as one course of an Italian meal.

clue.text: Very poor writer omitted chapter heading from novel

parts.note: a pen is something you write with

indicators.note: the chapter's first letter is left out of the word for novel

parts.note: novel as an adjective means new and strange, curious

indicators.note: the heading of chapter is its first letter

explanation.surface: A struggling author cutting a chapter heading from a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book but is the adjective, CURIOUS; 'omitted' removes its C.
explanation.definitionFit: Penurious means poverty-stricken, destitute.

clue.text: Top gymnast's composure

parts.note: PE, physical education, is a gymnast's subject at school
an ace is a top performer

explanation.surface: A star gymnast's calm.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as an ace at PE, a top gymnast.
explanation.definitionFit: Peace of mind is calmness, tranquillity.

clue.text: Harvester having no right to claim time off

parts.note: a sickle is a curved blade for harvesting

indicators.note: no means the right letter is absent from the claiming word

parts.note: to aver is to assert or claim

explanation.surface: A farmhand with no right to demand holidays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harvester' suggests a person, but it is the tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Sick leave is absence from work through illness, a kind of time away.

clue.text: Queen is introduced to each Liberal peer

indicators.note: the queen's letters are put inside each

explanation.surface: The monarch meets every Liberal member of the Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peer' suggests a lord; here it means an equal.
explanation.definitionFit: A peer in the sense of someone of the same standing is an equal.

clue.text: Following road to the north, rider goes astray in Scottish town

indicators.note: following means the rearranged rider comes after the road

parts.note: the A1 is Britain's Great North Road, written here as AI

indicators.note: going astray means wandering off course, so the letters of rider are jumbled

explanation.surface: A rider heads north up the main road and gets lost in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: The A1 runs from London to Edinburgh; its 1 reads as I. 'goes astray' makes RDRIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Airdrie is a town in North Lanarkshire, east of Glasgow.

clue.text: In court, English people stick together

indicators.note: the English people go in the court abbreviation

parts.note: men are people

explanation.surface: English people in a courtroom closing ranks.
explanation.definitionFit: To cement is to bind firmly, as mortar joins bricks.
